basic_identification.name: Spawning AI / Have I Been Trained
basic_identification.originator: Jordan Meyer (CEO), Mathew Dryhurst, Holly Herndon. Berlin/US-based artist-technologists. Herndon and Dryhurst are known for AI-collaborative music and art. Co-founded with two additional collaborators.
basic_identification.year: 2022 (Have I Been Trained launched September 2022); 2024 (Source.Plus marketplace launched)
basic_identification.geography: Berlin/US-based team. Global user base. Impact concentrated in Western art/tech communities. Partnerships with US-based platforms (ArtStation/Epic, Shutterstock, Stability AI, Hugging Face).

core_ideas.core_claim: Artists should have tools to understand, control, and consent to how their work is used in AI training datasets. Spawning builds the consent layer for AI, providing opt-out infrastructure (Have I Been Trained / Do Not Train registry) and opt-in infrastructure (Source.Plus ethical dataset marketplace). The core belief is that consent infrastructure will benefit both AI developers and the artists whose work trains their models.
core_ideas.medium_specificity: Entirely specific to the AI training data crisis. These tools exist because of the unique digital art problem: images posted online can be scraped and used to train generative AI models without consent, enabling models to reproduce artistic styles. This has no analog in traditional art. The tools address the specific technical challenge of identifying works in massive training datasets (LAION-5B: 5.85 billion image-text pairs) and communicating consent preferences to AI model trainers.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: Resistant to attention economy in purpose but operating within it for advocacy. Spawning's tools serve structural needs (consent, data sovereignty) rather than engagement metrics. However, the public awareness of training data issues was driven by attention-economy dynamics: viral Twitter threads, media coverage of artist outrage, and viral demonstrations of style mimicry. The movement needed attention to build political will for consent infrastructure.
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: Strongly intention-native. Built by artists to serve artists' declared needs. The tools address a structural gap (consent) rather than capturing engagement. Spawning explicitly states they believe consent infrastructure benefits the entire ecosystem, not just one side. The evolution from free opt-out (Have I Been Trained) to marketplace (Source.Plus) represents a shift toward sustainable intention-aligned infrastructure.

market_economics.revenue_model: Evolving. Initially bootstrapped, then $3M seed round (2023) led by True Ventures. Opt-out services are free. Evolving toward a marketplace model: Source.Plus offers curated, ethically sourced training datasets for AI developers, presumably with transaction or licensing fees. The revenue model is transitioning from grant/investment-sustained to marketplace-sustainable. Specific revenue figures not publicly available.
market_economics.market_position: Infrastructure layer between artists and AI model trainers. Consent middleware. Positioned as the neutral consent infrastructure that both sides need: artists need tools to exercise control; AI companies need legally defensible training data.
market_economics.price_range: Free for artist-facing tools (Have I Been Trained search, Do Not Train registry). Source.Plus marketplace pricing not publicly detailed. The value proposition for AI companies is legal/ethical risk reduction rather than a traditional product price.
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: Growing in adoption and scope. By early 2023, over 1 billion artwork opt-outs processed through partnerships with ArtStation and Shutterstock. Source.Plus launched June 2024 as ethical dataset marketplace. However, adoption by major AI companies (Midjourney, OpenAI, Google) remains voluntary and incomplete. The legal and regulatory environment is pushing demand for consent infrastructure. [uncertain]
market_economics.collector_demographics: N/A. This is infrastructure serving artists and AI companies, not a collecting platform.
market_economics.sustainability: Uncertain. The $3M seed provides runway but not long-term sustainability. Source.Plus marketplace model could be sustainable if AI companies adopt ethical data sourcing at scale. Regulatory pressure (EU AI Act, lawsuits) may force adoption. Risk: if AI companies develop their own consent solutions or regulations render the specific approach obsolete. The bootstrapped, artist-founded origin provides mission stability but limited financial resilience. [uncertain]

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Have I Been Trained: web-based search interface querying LAION-5B dataset via CLIP embeddings. Do Not Train registry: machine-readable opt-out preferences. Source.Plus: dataset marketplace with automated content classification (nudity, gore, PII detection), license validation, provenance tracking. Partnerships with Stability AI and Hugging Face for opt-out enforcement. Classifier models for content filtering.
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: Directly oppositional and constructive simultaneously. Oppositional: protesting unconsented use of art in AI training. Constructive: building infrastructure to make AI training ethical rather than blocking it entirely. The founders (Herndon and Dryhurst) are themselves AI art practitioners, which gives the project credibility and nuance: they are not anti-AI but pro-consent. This positions Spawning as building the ethical infrastructure the AI ecosystem needs rather than fighting it.
practice_aesthetics.liveness: Static infrastructure: database and registry tools. Not a creative or performative tool. The dynamic element is the ongoing negotiation between artists' consent preferences and AI companies' training practices.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: Not directly aesthetic. The relevant vocabulary is ethical/legal: consent, opt-in, opt-out, training data, data sovereignty, scraping, LAION, dataset, license compliance, do-not-train, data provenance, ethical sourcing. The project has contributed new terms to the art/AI discourse: 'consent layer,' 'do-not-train registry,' 'Source.Plus.'
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: Openness: building open tools for consent (Have I Been Trained is publicly accessible) while also creating a structured marketplace. Commons: contributing consent infrastructure as public good; Source.Plus introduces market logic. Infrastructure over spectacle: definitionally infrastructure. Individual artist agency: prioritizes individual artist consent decisions within a collective infrastructure.

infrastructure_governance.openness: Mixed. Have I Been Trained search is publicly accessible. The Do Not Train registry specification aims to be an open standard. Source.Plus is a proprietary marketplace. The underlying classifier models and dataset processing are proprietary. The project aims to create open consent standards while sustaining itself through proprietary services.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: Founding-team / startup. Decisions made by Meyer, Dryhurst, and Herndon with input from investors (True Ventures). No DAO or community governance structure. Artist input is gathered informally through community engagement rather than formal governance. The small team structure enables agility but creates dependency on founders.
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: Central to mission. Spawning exists to give artists data sovereignty over their work in AI training contexts. The Do Not Train registry is artist-controlled: artists decide whether their work can be used. Source.Plus validates licenses and provenance. However, enforcement depends entirely on AI companies voluntarily honoring the registry. Spawning cannot technically prevent a model trainer from using opted-out data; it can only make the information available and advocate for compliance.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Developing. The Do Not Train registry aims to be a universal standard that any AI company can check. Partnerships with Stability AI and Hugging Face demonstrate cross-platform potential. However, major players (OpenAI, Midjourney, Google) have not committed to the registry. Source.Plus provides an API for dataset access. The lack of universal adoption limits interoperability's practical impact.
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: Not directly relevant. Spawning preserves records of artist consent preferences but does not preserve artworks themselves. The registry creates a historical record of who opted out and when, which could serve future legal or historical purposes.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: This IS the consent architecture. Spawning's entire purpose is building consent infrastructure for AI training data. The architecture provides: (1) Transparency: search to discover if your work is in training sets. (2) Opt-out: register preference to be excluded from future training. (3) Opt-in: license work for AI training through Source.Plus. (4) Enforcement: voluntary compliance by partner companies. Weakness: the consent model is opt-out (presumed included unless you actively opt out), which does not meet GDPR's active consent standard. The Do Not Train registry approaches machine-readable consent but falls short of granular, context-specific consent.

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: Parallel but increasingly relevant. The traditional art world is aware of AI training data issues but relies on copyright law rather than technical consent infrastructure. Some galleries and institutions have expressed support for artist data rights without specifically adopting Spawning's tools. The project bridges the tech-art divide by addressing an issue that affects artists in all mediums whose work exists online.
field_position.what_it_enables: Artists can discover if their work is in AI training datasets. Artists can register opt-out preferences in a machine-readable format. AI companies can access ethically sourced, license-compliant training data through Source.Plus. The project creates precedent for artist-built infrastructure that addresses systemic power imbalances between individual creators and large technology companies.
field_position.what_it_lacks: Enforcement power: compliance is voluntary. Coverage of all major AI companies (OpenAI, Google, Midjourney not committed). Granular consent (binary opt-in/opt-out rather than nuanced permissions for specific uses). Retroactive remedy (cannot un-train a model). Financial compensation mechanism for artists whose work was already used. Clear legal identity verification for opt-out requests. Global reach beyond English-speaking art/tech communities. A model for compensating artists whose data has already been used.
field_position.who_is_excluded: Artists unaware the tools exist. Artists without English proficiency. Artists outside Western tech/art communities. Artists whose work was scraped from platforms not indexed by the search tool. Artists who lack the technical literacy to navigate opt-out processes. Communities in the Global South whose visual culture was scraped but who lack access to consent tools. Dead artists whose estates may not know about or engage with these tools.
field_position.frontier_signal: Frontier. Spawning represents the leading edge of consent infrastructure for AI training data. The concept is pioneering, but adoption, enforcement, and sustainability are unproven. The evolution from opt-out tool to ethical data marketplace (Source.Plus) represents a maturation of the model. Regulatory developments (EU AI Act, pending US legislation) could make this approach standard or supersede it with mandatory frameworks.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: Media coverage (TechCrunch, CNN, Ars Technica, MIT Technology Review), social media advocacy (Twitter/X art community), word of mouth among artists, conference presentations, artist community platforms (DeviantArt, ArtStation partnerships). Discovery was driven by the viral outrage over AI training data scraping in late 2022.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: Moderate. The project gained traction through social media attention to the training data controversy. Ongoing visibility depends on continued media coverage and artist advocacy. However, the core infrastructure (registry, marketplace) operates independently of social media attention. The regulatory environment provides an attention-independent driver of adoption.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Strongly intention-aligned. Built by artists to serve artists' structural needs. The mission (consent infrastructure) is field-serving rather than engagement-capturing. The evolution toward a marketplace introduces some market logic but the mission remains consent-first. This is one of the clearest examples of intention-native infrastructure in the digital art field.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: Significant. The search tool and opt-out registry are public goods. The concept of a do-not-train registry contributes to shared infrastructure. However, Source.Plus introduces enclosure: curated, ethically sourced data as a product. The tension between commons (free opt-out tools) and market (paid ethical data) is productive but real.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: Neither ownership nor meaning in the traditional sense. Spawning tracks a different kind of provenance: data provenance (where did this training data come from? was it consented?). This is provenance of usage rights rather than ownership or meaning. Source.Plus tracks image provenance (source, license, consent status) for training datasets.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: Present-focused with archival elements. The Do Not Train registry captures current consent preferences. Source.Plus validates current license status. No deep-historical analysis of how training data practices evolved. No anticipatory modeling of future consent needs. The temporal logic is reactive (responding to current crisis) rather than anticipatory.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: Addresses a specific, critical absence: the absence of consent in AI training data pipelines. The search tool reveals absence (your work is in the dataset without your knowledge or consent). However, it does not address the broader absence of structural power for individual artists in relation to technology companies, nor does it map the full landscape of what is missing from consent infrastructure.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Coherence around the principle that consent matters, without consensus on implementation details. The art community agrees that unconsented use is problematic but disagrees on solutions: some want full prohibition of scraping, others accept opt-out, others want compensation models, others want to abolish copyright entirely. Spawning navigates this by providing opt-in and opt-out options, letting artists make individual decisions within a shared framework.
coherence.contestability: Moderate. Artists can choose to opt in or out. The opt-out mechanism is voluntary for AI companies, making it contestable from the enforcement side. Criticism has been raised about the opt-out model itself (should the default be inclusion?) and about the identity verification process. The project is open to critique but governance is not community-controlled.
coherence.forkability: Partially forkable. The concept of a do-not-train registry could be replicated. The specific dataset search and processing infrastructure would be harder to fork without the LAION-5B index and partnerships. The marketplace (Source.Plus) depends on curated relationships. A competing consent infrastructure could emerge from regulators, other nonprofits, or platform-specific implementations.

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: The artist-built infrastructure precedent: practitioners identifying a structural need and building tools to address it. The dual approach of transparency (search/discover) and agency (opt-in/opt-out). The principle that consent should be machine-readable and interoperable. The credibility model: founded by AI art practitioners, not anti-technology campaigners. The ambition to build infrastructure that serves both sides of the artist-technology relationship.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: The opt-out default that presumes inclusion without consent. The binary consent model (in/out) that cannot express nuanced permissions. The dependency on voluntary corporate compliance for enforcement. The startup model that may prioritize growth metrics over mission fidelity. The geographic and linguistic limitations that exclude most of the world's artists from the consent infrastructure they need.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: Spawning builds consent infrastructure for how art is used (in AI training). A(DAI) builds knowledge infrastructure for how art is understood (in field intelligence). Both address structural power imbalances: Spawning between artists and AI companies; A(DAI) between practitioners and attention-economy platforms. The productive tension is that consent (Spawning) and context (A(DAI)) are complementary but different layers: an artist might consent to training but need context for what their work means. A(DAI) should understand Spawning as fellow infrastructure but should not reduce the consent question to a data field.

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: Spawning operates in and responds to the regulatory environment rather than being regulated itself. The EU AI Act's transparency and data governance requirements create demand for Spawning's tools. GDPR's consent requirements exceed Spawning's opt-out model (GDPR requires active consent, not just opt-out). Ongoing lawsuits (Getty v. Stability AI, Andersen v. Stability AI) could establish legal frameworks that either validate or supersede Spawning's approach. California AB 2013 requires AI training data disclosure, which aligns with Spawning's transparency mission.
regulatory_legal.ip_model: Spawning does not claim IP over artists' works. The infrastructure respects existing copyright: artists assert their rights through the registry. Source.Plus validates CC0 and other license compliance. The project operates within copyright law rather than creating a new IP model. However, the Do Not Train registry introduces a novel extra-legal consent mechanism that exists alongside (not within) formal copyright.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: Currently opt-out: artists are presumed included in training datasets unless they actively register an opt-out. Spawning acknowledges this is not ideal but pragmatic given the scale of existing datasets. Source.Plus represents a shift toward opt-in: a marketplace where data is explicitly licensed for training. The transition from opt-out (Have I Been Trained) to opt-in (Source.Plus) is the most important evolution in Spawning's model.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: Depends on partnerships with AI companies (Stability AI, Hugging Face) for opt-out enforcement. Depends on LAION-5B dataset access for search functionality. Source.Plus depends on building a marketplace with sufficient supply (consenting artists) and demand (AI companies). The project's impact depends on the voluntary ecosystem cooperating. No blockchain dependency; operates on traditional web infrastructure.
ecosystem.network_effects: Positive but slow. More artist opt-outs make the registry more comprehensive and valuable. More AI companies honoring the registry increases its credibility and attracts more artists. The 1 billion+ opt-outs through platform partnerships (ArtStation, Shutterstock) demonstrate potential network effects. However, without mandatory compliance, the network effects are limited by voluntary adoption.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: Independent of NFT crash. Spawning addresses the AI training data crisis, which accelerated after the NFT boom and continues regardless of NFT market conditions. The trajectory is upward, driven by regulatory pressure, ongoing lawsuits, and growing artist awareness. The shift to Source.Plus marketplace (June 2024) represents strategic maturation. The project's relevance grows as AI capabilities and training data demands increase.
